subject: Engineering decisions
title: `wf work <slug>` run mode (the git-state worker) in Rust
question: What was measured for `wf work <slug>` run mode (the git-state worker) in Rust?
workload: 2026-10-06: `wf work <slug>` run mode (the git-state worker) in Rust
method: Transcribed from the cited historical record. Units and precision follow the source.
finding: Not covered: live `rca run` runs, a lost lease during a long unit (heartbeat renewal races), the AIMD probe-up path (needs warm units older than 120 s). They keep the TS logic ported line for line but were not exercised against real load.

rows: Oracle: `work-run.integration.test.ts` (14 tests over a real bare origin and a real clone, `pnpm` stubbed). A TS seam makes it fast: `WF_WORKER_TICK_MS`, `WF_WORKER_LAUNCH_SPACING_MS` and `WF_WORKER_HEARTBEAT_MS` shrink the 15 s tick and 60 s launch spacing (unset in production). 14/14 on the TS bundle, then 14/14 on the Rust binary without a change. Covers landing two chained units, the prompt, a base that moved (rebase), a gate that never passes, an implementer that writes nothing, a failed dependency, a failing install released three times, a pre-failed unit, a live lease, a stale lease, an already landed plan, argument errors and SIGTERM. Whole integration suite after this: 584/584 on Rust; `cargo test` green.

Not covered: live `rca run` runs, a lost lease during a long unit (heartbeat renewal races), the AIMD probe-up path (needs warm units older than 120 s). They keep the TS logic ported line for line but were not exercised against real load.
Benchmark (`work p --once` on an already landed plan, n=5 median): TS 320 ms / 66 MB, Rust 71 ms / 12 MB (git calls dominate the Rust time).
